title: Cocoa vs. carob: nutrition differences

seo.title: Cocoa vs. carob: nutrition differences
seo.meta_description: Cocoa and carob can play similar roles in recipes, but differ sharply in fat, protein, natural sugar, fiber, caffeine, and flavor. Compare them per 100 g.
seo.search_intent: Compare the nutritional composition of cocoa powder and carob flour

excerpt: Carob is naturally much sweeter and almost fat-free; unsweetened cocoa has far more protein and fat and contains caffeine and theobromine. Both are fiber-rich by weight, but they do not taste or behave the same in recipes.
content_html:
Carob powder is often suggested as a cocoa substitute because it is brown, roasty, and useful in baked goods. Nutritionally, though, carob and cocoa are built very differently.

Compare the same weight

USDA reference data for unsweetened cocoa powder and carob flour make the contrast clear.

Per 100 gUnsweetened cocoaCarob flour
Calories228222
Protein19.6 g4.6 g
Fat13.7 g0.7 g
Carbohydrate57.9 g88.9 g
Sugars1.8 g49.1 g
Fiber37 g39.8 g

The calorie totals are surprisingly similar, but the sources are very different: cocoa carries much more fat and protein, while carob carries far more carbohydrate and naturally occurring sugar.

Carob is naturally sweet

Ripe carob pulp contains substantial sucrose, glucose, and fructose. That natural sweetness can let a recipe use less added sugar.

But “no added sugar” is not the same as sugar-free. The USDA carob entry has about 49 g sugar per 100 g, compared with under 2 g in unsweetened cocoa.

Cocoa is much higher in fat and protein

The cocoa reference contains 13.7 g fat/100 g versus just 0.65 g in carob—roughly a twentyfold difference. Protein is also much higher in cocoa, 19.6 g versus 4.6 g.

That matters more in a recipe using several ounces of powder than in a teaspoon sprinkled on top.

Both are high in fiber

This is where the two come surprisingly close: 37 g/100 g in cocoa and 39.8 g/100 g in carob in the reference entries. Real serving sizes are much smaller, but both can contribute meaningful fiber.

Caffeine and theobromine are a clear dividing line

Cocoa contains methylxanthines. The USDA cocoa entry has about 230 mg caffeine and more than 2,000 mg theobromine per 100 g. Studies of carob pulp, powder, and carob coffee have found both compounds below detection limits.

That makes carob useful for someone who wants a cocoa-like roasted flavor without cocoa's natural caffeine and theobromine.

Can you substitute carob one-for-one?

Sometimes, but expect a different result. Carob is sweeter, less bitter, and far lower in fat. Cocoa tastes darker and more astringent. A recipe may need less added sweetener when using carob, and liquid or fat may need adjustment.

The better choice depends on the goal: carob for natural sweetness and no methylxanthines; cocoa for true cocoa flavor and its characteristic nutrient profile.

faq.question: Is carob lower in calories than cocoa?
faq.answer: Not by much in the USDA references: 222 calories/100 g for carob flour versus 228 for unsweetened cocoa.

faq.question: Does carob contain sugar?
faq.answer: Yes. It is naturally sugar-rich; the USDA reference has about 49.1 g sugars per 100 g.

faq.question: Does carob contain caffeine?
faq.answer: Studies cited here found caffeine and theobromine below detection limits in carob pulp and common carob products.

faq.question: Which has more protein?
faq.answer: Unsweetened cocoa, at about 19.6 g/100 g versus 4.6 g/100 g in carob flour in the USDA references.
